supplementary_news.content: Politics Ground Reports Opinion National Interest PoV 50-Word Edit Defence Diplomacy India Economy ThePrint On Camera Videos In Pictures Society & Culture Around Town Book Excerpts Vigyapanti The Dating Story Health Science Science Tech World Events Off The Cuff The Speakers Bureau School of Journalism ThePrint Store More Judiciary Education YourTurn Work With Us Campus Voice Search Add ThePrint as a trusted source ✕ Youtube Twitter Instagram Facebook Whatsapp Telegram LinkedIn Tuesday, August 25, 2026 Politics Ground Reports Opinion National Interest PoV 50-Word Edit Defence Diplomacy India Economy ThePrint On Camera Videos In Pictures Society & Culture Around Town Book Excerpts Vigyapanti The Dating Story Health Science Science Tech World Events Off The Cuff The Speakers Bureau School of Journalism ThePrint Store More Judiciary Education YourTurn Work With Us Campus Voice Search Support our Journalism 9th Anniversary: Free Tote & Mug Subscribe HomeIndiaCapital fully equipped to deal with seasonal influenza cases: Delhi health minister India Capital fully equipped to deal with seasonal influenza cases: Delhi health minister PTI 21 August, 2026 07:51 pm IST Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Follow Us : Text Size: A- A+ New Delhi, Aug 21 (PTI) The capital has reported 2,392 influenza-A cases including 1,777 H1N1 (swine flu) infections so far this year, with Delhi Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh saying Friday that the city is fully equipped to deal with the seasonal rise in influenza cases. On the day, Singh attended a meeting chaired by Union Health Minister J P Nadda to review Delhi’s preparedness to treat seasonal influenza and vector-borne diseases. In an official statement issued after the meeting, Singh said there was no shortage of beds, doctors, medicines or essential medical equipment in the capital, adding that the patient tally was being monitored, and hospital arrangements being strengthened according to requirements. Show Full Article According to the statement, the Delhi State Health Mission is maintaining close surveillance through the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP), with daily monitoring of influenza-like illness (ILI), severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) and influenza cases reported through the IDSP-IHIP (Integrated Health Information Platform) portal. Regular updates are being shared with senior authorities. Advisories have been issued to chief district medical officers, district surveillance officers and hospitals for screening, reporting and monitoring of ILI, SARI and influenza cases, the statement said, adding that technical guidelines covering patient categorisation, treatment protocols, ventilatory management, masks and home care have also been circulated. Healthcare workers are being sensitised and trained on symptoms and follow-up protocols, while a refresher training programme for district officers was held recently, the statement said. An inter-sectoral meeting involving the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD), New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC), Delhi Cantonment Board, education department, Delhi Development Authority (DDA) and other stakeholders has directed that public awareness and IEC (information, education, and communication) activities on influenza prevention and control be intensified, it said. Of the total influenza-A cases, 1,777 were reported to be H1N1 infections, commonly known as swine flu, while 37 were H1, 138 were H3 and 440 were categorised as other influenza cases, according to the Delhi government. H1N1 is the predominant strain in the city. Additionally, Delhi has reported 246 dengue cases and 80 malaria cases this year, with zero deaths from either disease. Chikungunya cases stood at 19, also with no deaths. As part of vector-control measures, local bodies have conducted 2.38 crore house visits, sprayed 3.20 lakh houses, identified 91,217 mosquito-positive houses, issued 74,591 legal notices and launched 6,724 prosecutions, the statement said. Delhi has 35 designated sentinel surveillance hospitals, two apex referral laboratories at AIIMS and NCDC, and a malaria reference laboratory at Maulana Azad Medical College. Hospitals have been directed to maintain mosquito-free campuses, ensure timely reporting and keep adequate diagnostic kits, medicines, intravenous fluids, blood products and dedicated beds wherever required, the statement said. The Delhi government is coordinating with the MCD, NDMC, Delhi Cantonment Board and other departments for prevention and control, while dengue and malaria surveillance, training, awareness and door-to-door outreach through ASHA workers continue, it added. According to the statement, Delhi’s malaria annual parasite incidence remains below one, placing it in the pre-elimination phase, with the “Test, Track and Treat” strategy being implemented under the 2025-27 malaria elimination plan. The complete preparedness report of Delhi has been shared with Union Health Minister J P Nadda, including arrangements for beds, doctors, medicines and other essential facilities, Singh said, adding that the Union minister has assured that the Centre will provide every necessary support. Singh urged citizens to follow respiratory hygiene, use masks in crowded places, maintain hand hygiene, avoid close contact with people suffering from respiratory illnesses and consult doctors rather than self-medicate. “Public health preparedness is a continuous process. Our priority is early detection, timely treatment and ensuring adequate hospital capacity,” he added. PTI SGV ARB ARB This report is auto-generated from PTI news service. Delhi Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh also attended the meeting. Nadda reviewed the national surveillance and epidemiological situation, trends in influenza-like illness (ILI) and severe acute respiratory infection (SARI), testing and laboratory surveillance, and the preparedness of healthcare facilities to manage seasonal influenza cases. He stressed the need for close monitoring of influenza trends and the timely identification and management of any unusual increase or clustering of cases. The preparedness of healthcare facilities in Delhi was also reviewed, including the availability of hospital beds, critical care facilities, oxygen-supported beds, ventilators, essential medicines, diagnostics and other critical supplies. Nadda emphasised the need to maintain adequate surge capacity and seamless referral mechanisms, particularly for patients requiring specialised or critical care. Nadda called for continued strengthening of early detection, timely testing and appropriate clinical management of influenza cases, along with effective utilisation of the existing surveillance and laboratory network. On July 10, the Union Health Secretary wrote to all states and Union Territories, advising them to strengthen preparedness and surveillance for acute respiratory illness (ARI) and ensure that healthcare facilities remained adequately prepared. Nadda also emphasised the importance of public awareness and preventive health practices, including respiratory and hand hygiene. He advised people experiencing persistent or severe respiratory symptoms, breathing difficulty or other warning signs to seek medical advice promptly. The Union Health Minister reiterated that the situation was being closely and continuously monitored and stressed the need for sustained and coordinated efforts for prevention and control of seasonal diseases, including dengue and malaria. He called for a proactive and preparedness-oriented approach by state governments, with active participation of municipal councillors and other local bodies in generating awareness among communities about prevention, spread and control of seasonal diseases. Highlighting the increase in TB detection in the national capital through active involvement of local bodies and a whole-of-government approach, Nadda stressed the importance of public representatives at all levels disseminating factual and evidence-based information and strengthening community engagement. supplementary_news.content: News Business Arts & Culture Our Magazine Sports ET Scenes Haya Karima News Business Arts & Culture ET Scenes Our magazine Sports VACSERA to supply over 300,000 doses of seasonal Flu vaccine, says Health Ministry BY Egypt Today staff - Fri, 21 Aug 2026 - 02:25 GMT BY Egypt Today staff Fri, 21 Aug 2026 - 02:25 GMT CAIRO – 21 August 2026: The Ministry of Health and Population announced that the seasonal influenza vaccine will soon be available through the Holding Company for Biological Products and Vaccines (VACSERA), ahead of the winter season and the start of the school year. This initiative aims to safeguard public health and curb the spread of seasonal respiratory viruses. The Ministry highlighted that influenza remains among the most common respiratory illnesses, particularly in schools and crowded settings, underscoring the vital role of vaccination in preventing infection and reducing severe complications. To meet public demand, the Ministry affirmed its commitment to providing a variety of vaccines approved by the Egyptian Drug Authority—including trivalent and quadrivalent formulations—through VACSERA. The inventory exceeds 300,000 doses sourced from global suppliers, including French manufacturer Sanofi, American firm Abbott, and leading South Korean producers. VACSERA will begin rolling out the vaccines on September 1. They will be distributed across 28 centers affiliated with the Serum and Vaccine Institute across various governorates to ensure nationwide coverage. The Ministry noted that the vaccines offer effective immunity for over six months, providing robust protection throughout the flu season. Health authorities strongly encourage all citizens—especially children, the elderly, and individuals with chronic medical conditions—to get vaccinated at authorized centers to protect their families and strengthen community-wide immunity. Isha Deep August 24, 2026 Supported by Delhi has recorded 1,777 H1N1 cases up to August 20, 2026, amid a wider rise in seasonal influenza, but the ICMR has clarified that no new H1N1 strain has been detected in India. The circulating Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses are similar to the A/Missouri/11/2025 strain, have been circulating since 2025 and are well matched with vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere. The rise has nevertheless prompted closer monitoring. Union Health Minister JP Nadda reviewed the situation with Delhi Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh and senior officials, focusing on surveillance, testing, early detection and hospital preparedness. Delhi authorities have said hospitals have adequate beds, doctors, medicines and essential equipment. ICMR has stressed that seasonal influenza, including H1N1, is mostly self-limiting, but young children, older people and those with underlying medical conditions can face a higher risk of complications. The current message from health authorities is therefore one of caution without panic: the virus is not new, but a rise in infections still requires responsible monitoring and timely care. Delhi Sees A Sharp Rise In H1N1 Cases According to Delhi government data, 2,392 Influenza A cases had been recorded cumulatively by August 20, of which 1,777 were H1N1 infections. Another 210 cases were attributed to Influenza B, taking the combined Influenza A and B tally to 2,602. H1N1 has consequently emerged as the predominant Influenza A subtype in Delhi this year. The increase is particularly notable when compared with the 229 H1N1 cases recorded during the corresponding period last year. On August 20 alone, 114 new H1N1 cases were reported. The rise has been seen amid seasonal changes and an increase in people presenting with flu-like symptoms. Doctors have said most patients experience familiar influenza symptoms, including fever, cough, sore throat, headache and body aches. Dr Randeep Guleria has noted that H1N1 cases commonly increase during the monsoon, although the current numbers are relatively higher. Older people, young children and those with co-morbidities can be more vulnerable to complications, including breathing difficulties and viral pneumonia. The increase has also triggered a closer look at healthcare preparedness. On August 21, Nadda reviewed the situation and called for continued vigilance, robust surveillance and early identification of unusual increases or clusters. The review covered influenza-like illness and severe acute respiratory infection trends, testing and laboratory surveillance, as well as preparedness across healthcare facilities. ICMR Says No New H1N1 Strain Has Been Detected The rise in cases has naturally raised a key question: does the increase indicate that a new or more dangerous H1N1 virus is circulating? ICMR says no. Senior ICMR scientists have said the Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses currently circulating in India belong to the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like strain. The viruses belong to clade 6B.1A.5a2a and subclade D.3.1.1, and have been circulating since 2025. In other words, the current rise does not indicate the emergence of a newly detected H1N1 strain. ICMR has also said the circulating influenza strains are well matched with vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere. It has described seasonal influenza as mostly self-limiting, with most people recovering with appropriate care and rest. At the same time, reassurance does not mean the illness should be dismissed. Health authorities have specifically highlighted young children, older adults and people with underlying medical conditions as groups that can be more vulnerable to complications. Who Is At Risk H1N1 is a contagious respiratory infection. Influenza viruses primarily spread through respiratory droplets and particles released when an infected person coughs or sneezes. People can also become infected after touching contaminated surfaces and then touching their mouth or nose. An infected person may be able to spread influenza from about a day before symptoms appear and for several days afterwards. People who may face a greater risk of complications include: Young children, particularly those with underlying medical conditions. Older adults, who can be more vulnerable to severe influenza. People with underlying or chronic medical conditions, especially when these conditions affect the respiratory system or immune response. People with weakened immunity, who may have greater difficulty fighting infection. Pregnant women, who are generally considered a higher-risk group for complications from seasonal influenza. Risk also increases when someone has prolonged or close contact with an infected person, particularly in crowded or poorly ventilated environments. How Can You Stay Safe For most people, H1N1 does not require extensive medical intervention and recovery can occur with rest and appropriate supportive care. However, people at higher risk should seek medical advice early rather than waiting for symptoms to become severe. ICMR and NCDC guidance emphasises recognising warning signs and seeking timely medical care. Practical precautions include: Wash your hands regularly with soap and water or use an alcohol-based hand sanitiser. Cover your mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing. Avoid close contact with others when unwell, particularly vulnerable people. Stay home and rest while experiencing flu-like symptoms where possible. Avoid touching your eyes, nose and mouth with unwashed hands. Consider influenza vaccination after consulting a doctor, particularly if you belong to a higher-risk group. ICMR says the currently circulating strains are well matched with recommended Northern Hemisphere vaccine strains. Do not self-medicate with antibiotics, as they do not treat influenza viruses. Treatment decisions, including whether antiviral medicines are appropriate, should be made by a medical professional. People should seek prompt medical attention if they develop breathlessness, chest pain, low oxygen levels, confusion, severe weakness, dehydration or a persistent or worsening fever. NCDC guidance also identifies symptoms such as altered mental status, seizures, reduced urine output and breathing difficulty as warning signs requiring medical attention. Preparedness Matters Even Without A New Strain The government’s response reflects the distinction between a seasonal rise and the emergence of a new public-health threat. Nadda’s review focused not simply on case numbers but also on testing capacity, laboratory surveillance, hospital beds, critical-care facilities, oxygen-supported beds, ventilators, medicines and other essential supplies. The Union Health Ministry has said it is coordinating with states, hospitals and laboratories to strengthen surveillance, early detection and timely clinical management. Delhi’s health authorities have also sought to reassure residents about preparedness, saying hospitals have adequate capacity and that there is no shortage of beds, doctors, medicines or essential medical equipment. The broader lesson is that “no new strain” does not mean “no risk”. A familiar seasonal virus can still cause serious illness in vulnerable people, while a rise in cases can put additional pressure on healthcare systems. The Logical Indian’s Perspective The H1N1 situation shows why public-health communication must strike a careful balance between reassurance and responsibility. Rising numbers can understandably cause anxiety, but describing every surge as evidence of a dangerous new virus can create unnecessary fear; dismissing the increase altogether could leave vulnerable people without timely care. ICMR’s clarification provides reassurance, while continued surveillance and hospital preparedness ensure that reassurance is backed by action. In an age when health information can spread faster than the virus itself, how can we encourage a culture where evidence-based information, empathy and sensible caution replace both panic and complacency? The updated trivalent formulation targets two influenza A subtypes — A/H1N1 and A/H3N2 — and one influenza B/Victoria lineage virus, based on year-round surveillance data from the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) spanning more than 100 countries. Photo: Designed by Freepik by freepik, https://creativecommons.org/public-domain/pdm/ A sick woman Strain changes driven by antigenic drift Influenza viruses undergo continuous antigenic drift — gradual mutations in surface proteins hemagglutinin and neuraminidase that allow the virus to evade existing population immunity. When the antigenic distance between circulating viruses and vaccine strains exceeds a threshold, vaccine effectiveness drops sharply. WHO's February 2024 composition meeting concluded that all three components from the 2023–2024 vaccine no longer matched the dominant circulating strains. The A/H3N2 component, historically associated with more severe seasons and higher hospitalization rates in older adults, has been updated to a clade 2.3.4.4b virus (A/Thailand/8/2022-like) replacing the previous A/Darwin/9/2021-like strain. Clinicians note this subtype often drives earlier epidemic onset. The A/H1N1 component shifts to an A/Victoria/4897/2022-like virus (clade 5a.2a.1), while the B/Victoria component moves to a B/Austria/1359417/2021-like virus (clade V1A.3a.2). The B/Yamagata lineage, absent from global circulation since March 2020, remains excluded from trivalent formulations. Sequential waves and population risk Epidemiological patterns show influenza A typically dominates early season activity (September–January), while B/Victoria circulation increases toward spring (February–April). This sequential pattern creates compound risk for vulnerable groups — children, adults over 65, and persons with chronic respiratory or cardiovascular conditions — who may face a second wave after physiological reserves are depleted by an initial infection. "When different virus types circulate simultaneously, the risk of severe disease increases substantially," said therapist Anna Kuznetsova in an interview with Pravda.Ru. "It is like trying to extinguish two fires at opposite ends of a house — the body's resources are finite." General practitioner Elena Morozova added that the spring B-wave is frequently underestimated: "People relax, thinking winter is over, yet the virus finds new opportunities for spread." Clinical presentation and diagnosis All three strains present with the classic influenza syndrome: abrupt onset of fever (often above 38.5°C), myalgia, headache, and nonproductive cough. Clinical differentiation from other respiratory viruses or between influenza subtypes is unreliable without laboratory confirmation. PCR-based multiplex assays remain the diagnostic standard for specific subtype identification, though antiviral treatment decisions in high-risk patients are often made empirically based on clinical syndrome and local epidemiology. Vaccination timing and limitations Health authorities recommend vaccination from late August through October, allowing approximately two to three weeks for protective antibody development before community transmission accelerates in September with school and workplace reentry. A second activity peak typically follows the winter holiday period when contact rates surge again. Vaccine effectiveness varies annually (typically 40–60% against laboratory-confirmed infection when well-matched) and is lower against H3N2 due to its faster antigenic evolution and egg-adaptation changes during manufacturing. Vaccination does not guarantee prevention of infection but consistently reduces risk of hospitalization, intensive care admission, and death, particularly in older adults and those with comorbidities. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, August 24, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Technology Universal Flu Vaccine Protects Mice Against Multiple Strains by Bioengineer August 24, 2026 in Technology Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A vaccine built from genetically engineered baker’s yeast and decorated with a slow-changing influenza protein has protected mice against three influenza strains, according to researchers at the University of Michigan. The experimental formulation is designed to address one of the central weaknesses of seasonal flu vaccination: conventional vaccines focus largely on hemagglutinin, a highly variable surface protein that can change sufficiently from year to year to reduce the match between a vaccine and circulating viruses. By presenting the more conserved M2 protein in a virus-like structure, the researchers aim to stimulate immunity that could remain effective against a wider range of influenza A viruses, including strains that current vaccines do not anticipate. The findings are scheduled for presentation on Aug. 24 at the American Chemical Society’s fall 2026 meeting. They remain preclinical, and the results in mice do not establish that the vaccine will protect people or provide long-lasting immunity. Even so, the approach combines two goals that have long challenged influenza researchers: identifying a viral target that changes slowly enough to support broad protection, and developing a manufacturing system that can produce vaccine material rapidly when a new strain begins to spread. The project is led by Fei Wen, a professor of chemical engineering at the University of Michigan, with doctoral student Trang Hoang as first author. Seasonal influenza vaccines are updated because the virus continually evolves, particularly in hemagglutinin, or HA. This protein forms the majority of the virus’s external surface and is readily recognized by antibodies generated after infection or vaccination. Mutations in HA can alter the sites, known as epitopes, that antibodies bind, allowing new variants to partially escape pre-existing immunity. Global health authorities monitor influenza circulation and recommend vaccine compositions months before each flu season, giving manufacturers time to produce doses. The process can work well when forecasts are accurate, but protection may be reduced when an emerging strain differs substantially from the selected vaccine viruses. The Michigan team took a different approach by focusing on M2, a small influenza protein involved in the virus’s life cycle. M2 functions as an ion channel in the viral envelope, helping regulate acidity inside virus particles as they enter host cells. Because its structure and activity are constrained by the need to support viral replication, M2 generally tolerates fewer mutations than HA. The researchers specifically use the portion of M2 exposed on the exterior of the virus, often called the M2 ectodomain, as an antigen. This region is relatively conserved across influenza A viruses, although it is present in much smaller quantities than HA and therefore does not normally dominate the immune response to an inactivated flu virus. That limited natural visibility is one reason M2 has attracted interest as a universal-vaccine target. An immune response directed toward conserved M2 regions may recognize viruses from several influenza A subtypes, rather than responding narrowly to the HA and neuraminidase proteins of one seasonal strain. Such immunity would not necessarily prevent infection in the same way as highly strain-matched HA antibodies. Instead, antibodies and other immune mechanisms targeting M2 could interfere with viral spread or help immune cells identify infected cells more efficiently, potentially reducing disease severity and transmission. The exact balance of these protective mechanisms will need to be established in further animal studies and, eventually, human trials. To make M2 more immunologically visible, the researchers assembled it on virus-like particles, or VLPs. These particles imitate the approximate size and shape of a virus but contain no influenza genome, so they cannot replicate or cause influenza infection. Their repetitive, ordered surfaces can help cross-link receptors on immune cells and promote antigen uptake, making VLPs useful platforms for vaccine development. In this case, the particles are covered with M2 protein rather than displaying the full collection of proteins found on an infectious influenza virion. The design therefore concentrates the immune system’s attention on a target that is normally overshadowed by the much more abundant HA. The manufacturing method begins with ordinary baker’s yeast that has been genetically modified to produce large quantities of M2. The yeast is grown in a nutrient-rich liquid, allowing the engineered cells to synthesize the viral protein. Researchers then use mild chemical treatment to remove the rigid cell wall while preserving the cell membrane and the molecular machinery associated with particle formation. According to the team, the wall-less yeast cells bud off M2-bearing particles that can be collected and purified. This strategy uses yeast as a biological production platform rather than relying on influenza virus grown in eggs or cell culture, and it could make it easier to scale production without handling infectious virus. Speed is a major potential advantage of the platform. Traditional egg-based influenza manufacturing can require roughly six months because candidate viruses must be selected, adapted to grow efficiently in eggs, propagated, harvested, purified and formulated. Production timelines can be shorter with cell-based or recombinant systems, but each has its own technical and regulatory requirements. The Michigan researchers say their yeast-based process can generate a substantial amount of vaccine material in about a month. If validated at industrial scale, that turnaround could be valuable during an outbreak, when health authorities may need to respond to a newly recognized strain rather than wait for the next routine seasonal update. In mouse experiments, the M2-based VLP vaccine generated strong immune responses and protected animals challenged with three different influenza strains, the researchers report. The breadth of the protection is important because it suggests that the formulation can produce functional immunity beyond a single closely matched virus. However, animal challenge studies are an early stage of vaccine evaluation. The team’s next step is to determine how long protection lasts in vaccinated mice and to characterize the antibodies and cellular responses responsible for it. Researchers will also need to test dosing, safety, repeat vaccination, protection against additional influenza subtypes and performance in animal models that more closely predict human responses. The technology has been licensed to Esperovax, which is exploring development of an oral vaccine based on the platform. An oral formulation could simplify administration and potentially improve access, although delivering vaccine antigens through the digestive system presents its own challenges. Before the vaccine can be tested in people, the researchers must demonstrate consistent manufacturing, define the composition and purity of the particles, and complete the toxicology and regulatory studies required for clinical development. A broadly protective flu vaccine remains a long-term objective rather than an immediate clinical option, but the yeast-derived M2 particles offer a strategy that links conserved viral biology with rapid, potentially flexible production. Subject of Research: An experimental universal influenza vaccine using M2 protein-bearing virus-like particles produced in genetically engineered baker’s yeast. Read Today's Paper Delhi Swine Flu Cases: Over 2,300 Influenza-A cases reported; what people should know about the latest health advisory SECTIONS Delhi Swine Flu Cases: Over 2,300 Influenza-A cases reported; what people should know about the latest health advisory By Trending Desk , ET OnlineLast Updated: Aug 23, 2026, 09:07:00 AM IST Rate Story Follow us Share Font Size AbcSmall AbcMedium AbcLarge Save Print Comment Synopsis Delhi swine flu cases: Health department has issued an advisory urging people to maintain respiratory hygiene and avoid crowded places as influenza cases rise in the capital. Delhi has reported over 2,600 influenza cases this year, with H1N1 emerging as the dominant strain. Hospitals have been equipped to manage the seasonal increase in cases, while daily monitoring of influenza, influenza-like illness (ILI) and severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) cases is underway. Sign In What's Included Exclusive Stories Daily ePaper Access Smart Market Tools Curated Investment Ideas Ad-lite Experience Subscription Delhi swine flu cases The Delhi government has issued a health advisory urging residents to follow respiratory hygiene, avoid crowded places and seek timely medical attention as H1N1, commonly known as swine flu, cases continue to rise in the national capital. According to health department data cited by PTI, Delhi has reported 2,602 influenza cases this year, including 2,392 Influenza-A cases and 210 Influenza-B cases, as of Friday. Of the Influenza-A cases, 1,777 were H1N1. The department reported 159 new influenza cases on Thursday, including 114 H1N1 cases. Read more - Father paid Rs 2.9 lakh for son’s engineering admission, but he was stopped from taking the exam over unpaid fees; court orders college to pay Rs 2.27 lakh Delhi swine flu advisory: What people should do The health department has advised people to cover their mouth and nose while coughing or sneezing and wash their hands regularly with soap and water. Residents have also been asked to wear masks in crowded places and avoid close contact with people suffering from respiratory illnesses. People have been advised not to touch their eyes, nose or mouth unnecessarily, avoid spitting in public places and maintain adequate fluid intake. Live Events Read more - He scored 41 in Maths and 48 in Science in class 10; then changed his study habits, cracked JEE with 99.98 percentile & made it to IIT Bombay The advisory also urged people experiencing symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, breathing difficulty, body ache or headache to seek medical advice promptly rather than taking medicines without consulting a doctor. H1N1 cases dominate Delhi's influenza tally Of the 2,392 Influenza-A cases reported in Delhi this year, 1,777 are H1N1 cases, while 37 are H1 and 138 are H3 cases. Another 440 cases have been classified as other Influenza-A infections. The Influenza-B tally includes 200 Victoria strain cases and 10 other cases. On Thursday, Delhi recorded 155 Influenza-A cases, including 114 H1N1 cases, two H1 cases, one H3 case and 38 other Influenza-A cases. Four Influenza-B cases were also reported. Delhi hospitals prepared to handle seasonal influenza The health department said Delhi is fully prepared to deal with the seasonal increase in influenza cases, with adequate beds, doctors, medicines and essential medical equipment available across hospitals. A total of 35 hospitals have been placed under special surveillance, while two referral laboratories at AIIMS and the National Centre for Disease Control have been designated for testing and monitoring. Technical guidelines have also been issued covering patient categorisation, treatment protocols, ventilatory management, mask use and home care. Hospitals asked to monitor flu and respiratory infections The department has issued advisories to chief district medical officers, district surveillance officers and hospitals on screening, reporting and monitoring cases of influenza-like illness (ILI), severe acute respiratory infection (SARI), influenza and COVID-19 through the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP). Healthcare workers are also being trained on existing guidelines, symptoms and signs of respiratory illnesses and the follow-up measures required for patients. Delhi Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh attended a meeting chaired by Union Health Minister J P Nadda on Friday to review the capital's preparedness for seasonal influenza and vector-borne diseases. Singh said there was no shortage of beds, doctors, medicines or essential medical equipment in Delhi, adding that patient numbers were being monitored and hospital arrangements were being strengthened according to requirements. Delhi monitoring influenza cases daily The Delhi State Health Mission is monitoring the influenza situation through the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP), with daily data on influenza, ILI and SARI cases being tracked through the IDSP-IHIP portal. A daily bulletin is prepared and shared with senior authorities, while daily review meetings are being held with chief district medical officers to assess the situation. An inter-sectoral meeting was also held on August 20 with officials from the MCD, NDMC, Cantonment Board, Education Department and DDA. The departments were directed to strengthen public awareness and information, education and communication measures to prevent and control seasonal influenza. Health facilities and hospitals are conducting awareness sessions in outpatient departments and displaying IEC material. A refresher training session for district officers was held on August 17 to discuss the current influenza situation, case definitions and treatment. Who is most vulnerable to seasonal influenza? Seasonal influenza is an acute respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses that circulate worldwide. Young children and elderly people with underlying health conditions are among those considered more vulnerable to severe infection, according to the health department. India generally experiences two seasonal influenza peaks each year, between January and March and during the post-monsoon period. While H1N1 is the predominant influenza subtype in Delhi this year, H3N2 was the predominant subtype in the capital last year, the department said. The health authorities said surveillance guidelines remain in place throughout the year, with measures being taken to monitor, prevent and control the spread of influenza. supplementary_news.content: Home News Obituary Recipes Charity Special ಕನ್ನಡ Live TV RADIO Advertise Contact Us Matrimonial Properties Jobs General Ads Red Chillies Music Ask Dr Greetings Astrology Tribute Of Love Latest DRC Ebola outbreak crosses 5,500 cases, deaths top 2,600 Mon, Aug 24 Centre restricts cold medicines containing two drugs for children below 4 Mon, Aug 24 Experts finalise national guidelines to prevent fatty liver disease Mon, Aug 24 AI framework detects cancer stem cells, new drug targets tumour cells Mon, Aug 24 Safdarjung Hospital performs first robot-assisted knee replacement Sun, Aug 23 Physical inactivity: The silent driver of lifestyle diseases Sun, Aug 23 H1N1 cases rise in India as doctors stress annual flu vaccination Sun, Aug 23 Health H1N1 cases rise in India as doctors stress annual flu vaccination Sun, Aug 23 2026 03:27:36 PM Daijiworld Media Network - New Delhi New Delhi, Aug 23: India is witnessing a rise in H1N1 cases, with Delhi emerging as one of the key hotspots this season, prompting health authorities to strengthen surveillance and issue an advisory. Doctors are also stressing the importance of annual influenza vaccination, particularly for people at higher risk of developing complications. Commonly known as swine flu, H1N1 emerged in 2009 and was initially associated with influenza viruses found in pigs, which led to its popular name. The virus subsequently established sustained transmission among humans and now circulates as seasonal influenza A(H1N1)pdm09. According to Delhi Health Department data, the national capital had reported 1,777 H1N1 cases as of August 20, including 114 new cases in a single day. Delhi had recorded 2,602 influenza cases overall, of which 2,392 were Influenza-A and 210 were Influenza-B. The increase prompted the Delhi government to issue a health advisory and step up surveillance, while Union Health Minister JP Nadda reviewed the situation and the preparedness of hospitals. Dr Rajeev Chowdry, Director of Internal Medicine at Yatharth Hospital, Faridabad, said modern seasonal flu vaccines are designed to protect against the influenza viruses that surveillance indicates are most likely to circulate during the upcoming season. The H1N1 component is included alongside H3N2 and influenza B components in current trivalent influenza vaccines. H1N1 is a subtype of influenza A. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses currently circulating among humans are descendants of the virus that emerged in 2009. Like other influenza viruses, they have continued to undergo genetic and antigenic changes. This continuous evolution is one of the main reasons influenza vaccination is recommended every year. The virus circulating during one season may not be antigenically identical to strains that circulated in previous years. The World Health Organization therefore conducts global influenza surveillance and recommends vaccine compositions twice a year, separately for the northern and southern hemispheres, to ensure the best possible match with circulating strains. For the 2026-27 northern hemisphere influenza season, the WHO recommendation includes an H1N1pdm09-like strain in both egg-based and cell-culture or recombinant vaccines. The flu vaccine works by exposing the immune system to influenza antigens, allowing the body to develop antibodies without causing influenza infection from the vaccine itself. Following vaccination, the body needs time to develop protection, with the CDC stating that it generally takes around two weeks for protective antibodies to develop. Getting vaccinated before influenza activity becomes widespread is therefore preferable. Dr Chowdry said vaccination can reduce the risk of developing influenza and can also reduce the likelihood of severe disease if infection occurs. However, vaccination does not guarantee that a person will never contract influenza. Vaccine effectiveness varies from season to season depending on factors such as the match between vaccine strains and circulating viruses, the person's age and immune response and the particular influenza strain involved. “But vaccination can still reduce the risk of severe outcomes,” Dr Chowdry said. H1N1 symptoms are broadly similar to those caused by other seasonal influenza infections. People may develop fever, sore throat, cough, body aches, headache, chills and fatigue. In some cases, influenza can progress to serious complications such as pneumonia and respiratory failure. WHO India describes influenza as a contagious respiratory illness that can range from mild to severe. Severe infection can result in hospitalisation or death, with young children, pregnant women, older adults and people with certain underlying health conditions facing a higher risk of complications. The WHO estimates that seasonal influenza causes around one billion cases globally every year, including three to five million cases of severe illness and between 290,000 and 650,000 respiratory deaths annually. H1N1 spreads in much the same way as other seasonal influenza viruses. An infected person can release respiratory particles while coughing, sneezing or talking, which may then be inhaled by people nearby. Close contact with an infected person and contaminated hands or surfaces can also contribute to transmission. Dr Chowdry said the virus is highly contagious and can survive in the environment for a period of time. He also stressed that H1N1 spreads from person to person and is not acquired by eating properly cooked pork products. Annual vaccination is recommended because immunity can decline over time and influenza viruses continue to evolve. The WHO considers health workers, older adults, pregnant women and people with certain chronic medical conditions among the priority groups for seasonal influenza vaccination. People with conditions affecting the lungs, heart, kidneys, liver, nervous system or metabolism may face a greater risk of complications. Those with weakened immune systems are also more vulnerable, while children and older adults remain important groups because severe influenza can disproportionately affect them. Health authorities generally recommend getting vaccinated before influenza activity rises in a particular area, while allowing around two weeks for the immune response to develop. CDC guidance says September and October are generally suitable months for vaccination in the northern hemisphere, although vaccination can continue later while influenza viruses are circulating. Dr Chowdry advised people, especially those at higher risk of complications, to discuss the appropriate timing and vaccine formulation with their doctor. Along with vaccination, maintaining basic respiratory hygiene can help reduce transmission. Regular handwashing with soap and water or an alcohol-based hand sanitiser, along with avoiding close contact with people who are coughing or showing flu-like symptoms, can reduce the risk of infection. People who develop significant flu symptoms, particularly those at higher risk of complications, should not automatically assume they have a routine cold. Early medical assessment can be important in severe, progressive or high-risk cases, as antiviral medicines may be useful when influenza infection is suspected or confirmed and treatment is medically indicated. supplementary_news.content_title: Karnataka records 4,212 influenza cases; Health Dept says H1N1 rise is seasonal
supplementary_news.content: Kerala Karnataka records 4,212 influenza cases; Health Dept says H1N1 rise is seasonal With Karnataka reporting 4,212 influenza cases so far this year, the Health Department has stepped up surveillance and preparedness measures while saying the current H1N1 rise is within the state’s normal seasonal pattern. Karnataka has recorded 4,212 laboratory-confirmed influenza cases across 32 districts so far this year, with the Health Department attributing the current rise in H1N1 cases to the state’s usual seasonal pattern and urging people not to panic. According to surveillance data from the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP), 4,212 influenza cases had been confirmed in the state as of August 22, 2026. H1N1 is a strain of the influenza A virus that can cause seasonal flu. Common symptoms include fever, cough, sore throat, body ache and fatigue. Bengaluru accounts for the majority of the cases. The Greater Bengaluru Authority (MSU) area has reported 2,070 cases so far this year, compared to 2,587 in 2025 and 1,189 in 2024. Bengaluru Urban has recorded 1,011 cases, broadly comparable to 961 cases in 2025 and 991 in 2024. The Health Department said influenza generally records two seasonal peaks in Karnataka — between January and March and again between July and September. The current increase in cases therefore falls within the state's usual seasonal pattern. Health Minister UT Khader chaired a review meeting with senior health officials from the state and districts to assess preparedness to manage the seasonal rise in influenza. The department said government health facilities have adequate infrastructure, essential medicines and other supplies to handle a possible increase in cases. Surveillance for Influenza-Like Illness (ILI) and Severe Acute Respiratory Infection (SARI) has also been strengthened in line with guidelines issued by the World Health Organization and the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Surveillance is being carried out through designated sentinel sites under the ICMR-NCDC network for pan-respiratory virus surveillance, as well as through the Viral Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDL) network. The department said laboratories have sufficient consumables to ensure timely sample collection and testing. Health facilities have been directed to maintain adequate stocks of essential supplies, including personal protective equipment, N95 masks and Oseltamivir, an antiviral medication used to treat influenza. Healthcare workers have also been sensitised to identify ILI and SARI cases early, assess risk and provide appropriate treatment. Private hospitals and healthcare facilities have been asked to follow state protocols for screening, testing and treatment of H1N1 cases. They have also been directed to report confirmed cases to surveillance authorities through the IHIP platform. As part of efforts to prevent transmission, the department has reinforced respiratory and hand hygiene measures in healthcare facilities and stepped up public awareness campaigns through print, electronic and social media. The Health Department has advised people to cover their nose and mouth while coughing or sneezing, wash their hands regularly with soap and water, drink plenty of fluids and isolate themselves if they develop flu-like symptoms. People have also been advised to avoid touching their eyes, nose and mouth, refrain from self-medication, and avoid crowded places, unnecessary gatherings and shaking hands while symptomatic. The department has also advised against reusing napkins. People experiencing symptoms have been advised to seek care at the nearest government health facility. The Health Department said there was no need for panic over the rise in cases, but urged people to follow recommended precautions and seek timely medical attention to help limit the spread of seasonal influenza. Karnataka has recorded 4,212 laboratory-confirmed influenza cases across 32 districts so far this year, with the Health Department attributing the current rise in H1N1 cases to the state’s usual seasonal pattern and urging people not to panic. According to surveillance data from the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP), 4,212 influenza cases had been confirmed in the state as of August 22, 2026. H1N1 is a strain of the influenza A virus that can cause seasonal flu. Common symptoms include fever, cough, sore throat, body ache and fatigue. Bengaluru accounts for the majority of the cases. The Greater Bengaluru Authority (MSU) area has reported 2,070 cases so far this year, compared to 2,587 in 2025 and 1,189 in 2024. Bengaluru Urban has recorded 1,011 cases, broadly comparable to 961 cases in 2025 and 991 in 2024. The Health Department said influenza generally records two seasonal peaks in Karnataka — between January and March and again between July and September. The current increase in cases therefore falls within the state's usual seasonal pattern. Health Minister UT Khader chaired a review meeting with senior health officials from the state and districts to assess preparedness to manage the seasonal rise in influenza. The department said government health facilities have adequate infrastructure, essential medicines and other supplies to handle a possible increase in cases. Surveillance for Influenza-Like Illness (ILI) and Severe Acute Respiratory Infection (SARI) has also been strengthened in line with guidelines issued by the World Health Organization and the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Surveillance is being carried out through designated sentinel sites under the ICMR-NCDC network for pan-respiratory virus surveillance, as well as through the Viral Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDL) network. The department said laboratories have sufficient consumables to ensure timely sample collection and testing. Health facilities have been directed to maintain adequate stocks of essential supplies, including personal protective equipment, N95 masks and Oseltamivir, an antiviral medication used to treat influenza. Healthcare workers have also been sensitised to identify ILI and SARI cases early, assess risk and provide appropriate treatment. Private hospitals and healthcare facilities have been asked to follow state protocols for screening, testing and treatment of H1N1 cases. They have also been directed to report confirmed cases to surveillance authorities through the IHIP platform. As part of efforts to prevent transmission, the department has reinforced respiratory and hand hygiene measures in healthcare facilities and stepped up public awareness campaigns through print, electronic and social media. The Health Department has advised people to cover their nose and mouth while coughing or sneezing, wash their hands regularly with soap and water, drink plenty of fluids and isolate themselves if they develop flu-like symptoms. People have also been advised to avoid touching their eyes, nose and mouth, refrain from self-medication, and avoid crowded places, unnecessary gatherings and shaking hands while symptomatic. The department has also advised against reusing napkins. People experiencing symptoms have been advised to seek care at the nearest government health facility. The Health Department said there was no need for panic over the rise in cases, but urged people to follow recommended precautions and seek timely medical attention to help limit the spread of seasonal influenza. supplementary_news.content: Home Mail News NewsBusinessMoviesCricketSportsGetahead Money Money HomeNewsForexIndicesMutual FundsInsuranceGainersLosers TrendsStar PortfoliosMy PortfolioMy Watchlist BusinessEmailGurusTV More News > Headlines Defence Images Columns Interviews Specials Coverage Videos Archives Business > Headlines Columns Specials Personal Finance Interviews Images Technology Auto Union Budget 2026 Archives Movies > Headlines Images Interviews Reviews Web Series Videos South Cinema Quiz Hollywood Archives Cricket > Headlines Images Stats Women's T20 WC 2026 WT20 2026: Games, Players, Teams IPL 2026 Archives Sports > Headlines Formula 1 Football Tennis Chess Hockey Get Ahead > Headlines Specials Careers Glamour Health Achievers Finance Travel Food Videos Gadgets Biking Relationships Archives Money > News Forex Indices Sectors Mutual Funds Insurance Gainers Losers Trends Star Portfolios My Portfolio My Watchlist More Mail Business Email Gurus TV Rediff Podcast Astrology Home » News » H1N1 cases rise in Delhi, North India; experts say virus not more virulent H1N1 cases rise in Delhi, North India; experts say virus not more virulent By Satyam Dvivedi August 24, 2026 22:45 IST 4 Minutes Read Listen to this article Watch on Rediff TV Share this Article x As H1N1 influenza cases surge across Delhi and North India, health experts are urging high-risk individuals to take precautions while confirming the virus is a known strain and not more virulent. IMAGE: Union Health Minister JP Nadda chairs a review meeting on the H1N1 influenza preparedness, in New Delhi, August 21, 2026Photograph: @MoHFW_INDIA X/ANI Photo Key Points H1N1 influenza cases are increasing in Delhi and North India, consistent with seasonal flu activity. Experts confirm the H1N1 strain is not new or more virulent, alleviating panic. High-risk groups, including the elderly, young children, pregnant women, and those with chronic illnesses, should take extra precautions. Symptoms often include fever, cough, and body ache; severe warning signs like breathlessness require immediate medical attention. Most H1N1 infections are mild and self-limiting, resolving within three to five days with rest and hydration. H1N1 influenza cases have increased in Delhi and parts of North India in recent weeks, with experts advising people, particularly those at higher risk of complications, to take precautions but stressed that there is no evidence of the virus becoming more virulent. Understanding The H1N1 Strain Speaking to PTI Videos, former WHO chief scientist and former ICMR director general Dr Soumya Swaminathan said H1N1 is a known strain of influenza and not a new virus. "There is no evidence of a major antigenic shift or that the virus has become more virulent or dangerous," Dr Swaminathan said, adding that the recent increase in cases was consistent with seasonal influenza activity, particularly during the monsoon and winter months. The strain that caused the 2009 swine flu pandemic has continued to circulate globally. Swaminathan said that most people recover from the infection with adequate rest, fluids and symptomatic treatment. Who Is At Risk And What Are The Symptoms? However, elderly people, children, particularly those below five years of age, pregnant women and those with underlying chronic illnesses are at greater risk of complications. Warning signs such as breathlessness, bluish lips or nails, inability to eat or drink, altered consciousness, rapid breathing, vomiting or unusual irritability in children warrant prompt medical attention, Swaminathan said. Former AIIMS director Dr Randeep Guleria said H1N1 cases were currently rising in Delhi but were expected to decline as the monsoon recedes. He advised people, especially those in high-risk groups, to take precautions against influenza infection. Physician, public health and health policy expert Dr Chandrakant Lahariya said H1N1 was not a new influenza subtype. People with diabetes, hypertension or obesity, along with pregnant women, elderly persons and children, may be at higher risk of complications, he said. Those experiencing flu-like symptoms such as fever, cough, headache and body ache should consult a doctor and avoid taking antibiotics unless prescribed, Lahariya said. Patients should get adequate rest, stay hydrated, maintain electrolyte balance and ensure sufficient food intake during the illness, he added. Recognising Severe Complications Severe influenza can lead to complications such as pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and, in some cases, brain infection, said Dr Rashmi Kapoor, head of the Department of Paediatrics at Regency Healthcare, Kanpur. Parents should ensure that children remain adequately hydrated and seek immediate medical attention if they develop breathing difficulties or seizures, Kapoor said. She also advised parents to consider seasonal flu vaccination for children. Expert Advice And Public Reassurance Dr Abhishek Tandon, consultant in respiratory and sleep medicine at Medanta, Lucknow, said H1N1 influenza was widespread in north India but there was no need to panic. Most cases present as a mild and self-limiting upper respiratory infection, with symptoms including fever, sneezing, runny nose, sore throat, dry cough, breathlessness, weakness and fatigue, he said. Tandon advised against taking antibiotics or steroids over the counter and said high-risk patients and those with underlying health conditions may require antiviral treatment, such as oseltamivir, following medical consultation. Most infections resolve within three to five days, Tandon said. On Sunday, ICMR sources said that no new strain of H1N1 has been identified and there is no cause for panic. The Influenza strains currently circulating are "well matched with the vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere", they said. "The rise in H1N1 cases has brought preventive vaccination back into the conversation," said Dr Bharat Gopal, senior director, Respiratory and Sleep Medicine, Medanta Mediclinic, Defence Colony and Medanta-The Medicity. supplementary_news.content_title: No new H1N1 strain in India, existing vaccines sufficient, says ICMR
supplementary_news.content: The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) on Sunday (August 23, 2026) said that the Influenza A (H1N1) viruses currently circulating in the country belong to the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1) pdm09-like virus strain. It clarified that no new strain of H1N1 has been identified and there is no cause for panic. “These viruses belong to clade 6B.1A.5a2a, subclade D.3.1.1, and have been in circulation since 2025. The Influenza strains currently circulating are also well matched with the vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere,” ICMR said. “Seasonal influenza, including H1N1, is mostly self-limiting,” it added. Common symptoms of the illness include fever, cough, headache, and body ache, and most people recover with appropriate care and rest. However, young children, elderly persons, and individuals with underlying medical conditions may be at a greater risk of complications. If symptoms persist, worsen, or become severe, consultation with a doctor is advised, it said. The Union Health Ministry has said that it is closely monitoring the situation through regular surveillance and is undertaking necessary public health measures. India has registered a rise in seasonal Influenza A(H1N1) cases, commonly called swine flu, this monsoon, especially in major cities. Delhi has reported 1,777 confirmed H1N1 cases so far this year, including 114 new cases on August 20. Karnataka has registered over 4,000 cases, with more than half reported from Bengaluru. Rising influenza activity has also been reported in Mumbai, Chennai and parts of Kerala. National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) data show that H1N1 activity was relatively low in 2021 (778 cases, 12 deaths) after the pandemic period, but rebounded sharply in 2022 (13,202 cases, 410 deaths) and remained substantial in 2023 (8,125 cases, 129 deaths). By June 2024, India had already recorded 7,215 cases and 150 deaths, and year-end numbers were higher. NCDC’s 2025 reporting shows that H1N1 continued to circulate across multiple States. NCDC maintains a nationwide influenza surveillance network and publishes State-wise data and H1N1 treatment/prevention guidelines. It recommends seasonal influenza vaccination based on WHO strain recommendations. For the 2025–26 season, India’s recommended trivalent vaccine included H1N1, H3N2 and B/Victoria components, with circulating Indian H1N1 strains aligning with vaccine strains. “People at higher risk should consider annual vaccination and seek medical advice promptly if flu symptoms become severe,” Anil Bansal of the Delhi Medical Association said. India World Sport Data Health Opinion Science Entertainment Premium Videos Podcast Photos Visual Stories Specials TH Explains eBooks TH Games Newsletter Lit For Life The Huddle Home Sci-Tech Health No new H1N1 strain in India, existing vaccines sufficient, says ICMR Influenza strains currently circulating are well matched with the vaccine strains, and the seasonal flu is self-limiting, ICMR said, adding that people with underlying medical conditions are at risk of complication Updated - August 23, 2026 10:06 pm IST - New Delhi Bindu Shajan Perappadan READ LATER SEE ALL Remove Image used for representational purposes only. | Photo Credit: Getty Images/iStockphoto The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) on Sunday (August 23, 2026) said that the Influenza A (H1N1) viruses currently circulating in the country belong to the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1) pdm09-like virus strain. It clarified that no new strain of H1N1 has been identified and there is no cause for panic. H1N1 cases on the rise, experts say no cause for alarm “These viruses belong to clade 6B.1A.5a2a, subclade D.3.1.1, and have been in circulation since 2025. The Influenza strains currently circulating are also well matched with the vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere,” ICMR said. “Seasonal influenza, including H1N1, is mostly self-limiting,” it added. Common symptoms of the illness include fever, cough, headache, and body ache, and most people recover with appropriate care and rest. However, young children, elderly persons, and individuals with underlying medical conditions may be at a greater risk of complications. If symptoms persist, worsen, or become severe, consultation with a doctor is advised, it said. H1N1 surge: hospital footfall increases as doctors flag risks The Union Health Ministry has said that it is closely monitoring the situation through regular surveillance and is undertaking necessary public health measures. India has registered a rise in seasonal Influenza A(H1N1) cases, commonly called swine flu, this monsoon, especially in major cities. Delhi has reported 1,777 confirmed H1N1 cases so far this year, including 114 new cases on August 20. Karnataka has registered over 4,000 cases, with more than half reported from Bengaluru. Rising influenza activity has also been reported in Mumbai, Chennai and parts of Kerala. National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) data show that H1N1 activity was relatively low in 2021 (778 cases, 12 deaths) after the pandemic period, but rebounded sharply in 2022 (13,202 cases, 410 deaths) and remained substantial in 2023 (8,125 cases, 129 deaths). By June 2024, India had already recorded 7,215 cases and 150 deaths, and year-end numbers were higher. NCDC’s 2025 reporting shows that H1N1 continued to circulate across multiple States. NCDC maintains a nationwide influenza surveillance network and publishes State-wise data and H1N1 treatment/prevention guidelines. It recommends seasonal influenza vaccination based on WHO strain recommendations. For the 2025–26 season, India’s recommended trivalent vaccine included H1N1, H3N2 and B/Victoria components, with circulating Indian H1N1 strains aligning with vaccine strains. “People at higher risk should consider annual vaccination and seek medical advice promptly if flu symptoms become severe,” Anil Bansal of the Delhi Medical Association said. Akriti Anand Published24 Aug 2026, 11:25 AM IST H1N1 Cases near 1,800 in Delhi: Why Is the Health Minister Holding a Meeting Today? Explained AI Quick Read Scientists at the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) clarified on Sunday that no new strain of Influenza A (H1N1, also known as swine flu) has been identified in the country. “The influenza A [H1N1] pdm09 viruses currently circulating in India are similar to the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1) pdm09-like virus strain. These viruses belong to clade 6B.1A.5a2a and subclade D.3.1.1 and have been in circulation since 2025,” an ICMR scientist told news agency PTI. “There is no cause for panic,” the ICMR scientist said as Delhi saw a spike in H1N1 cases. The national capital has recorded over 2,300 influenza A cases this year, including over 1,777 H1N1 (swine flu) cases till Friday, news agency PTI reported. The health department said 114 H1N1 cases were reported on Thursday alone. H1N1 is “mostly self-limiting”. However, children, elderly people and those with underlying conditions face higher risks. Common symptoms include fever, cough, headache and body ache. Most people recover with appropriate care and rest, the scientists said. They also advised people to consult a doctor if symptoms persist, worsen or become severe. The scientists, as per the ICMR, also said that the influenza strains currently circulating are well-matched to the vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere. H1N1, commonly known as swine flu, is a type A influenza virus that causes respiratory infections. Here's all you need to know about the H1N1 flu vaccine: Who can take it? When can it be administered? Why do you need it? Why is the H1N1 vaccine important? Director General of Health Services (DGHS) Dr Loveneesh G Krishna told news agency ANI last week that vaccination can help decrease the severity of H1N1 infection. Vaccination is a “preventive measure”, and not a cure altogether. It helps your body build immunity, so you are less likely to get sick with the H1N1 virus in the first place. “H1N1 is a seasonal influenza that spreads very easily from one person to another. Therefore, we need to take some preventive measures, which include wearing a mask to cover your nose and mouth, washing your hands frequently with soap and water, keeping indoors well-ventilated, and taking vaccines to decrease the severity,” Krishna was quoted as saying. “The flu vaccine is the best protection against the flu. If you get the flu vaccine, you are 60% less likely to need treatment for the flu,” Max Healthcare explained on its website. Vaccination is not a recommended intervention for swine flu-infected patients. Which influenza vaccine to take? Who can take them? The ICMR said in a statement on Sunday that circulating H1N1 strains match the recommended Northern Hemisphere vaccine strains. The National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) has also recommended the use of the “NH [Northern Hemisphere]” vaccine in the 2026-2027 influenza season. 1. NASOVAC-S4: Influenza Vaccine (Human, Live Attenuated) I.P. Seasonal, Quadrivalent (Liquid) Intranasal > Recommended for individuals aged 2 years or older; for intranasal administration as a spray. The nasal spray vaccine is not recommended for people with some medical conditions. Also, if you are pregnant, you should not get the nasal spray flu vaccine. > Single intranasal dose of 0.5 ml is administered as 0.25 ml per nostril. View full Image Credit: Serum Institute of India 2. VaxiFlu S: Trivalent Influenza vaccine -contains two A types (H1N1 & H3N2) and one B type (Victoria); Inactivated influenza vaccine (NA). > Recommended for children above 6 months of age, for adults and seniors as an annual shot; to be administered "intramuscularly" by a trained healthcare professional. Kindly do not self-administer. > For children between 6 months to 9 years of age: Children who have not previously been vaccinated against influenza, two doses should be given at an interval of at least 4 weeks. For children who have been vaccinated against influenza earlier, a single dose is recommended every year. > For children above 9 years of age, adults and seniors: A single dose is recommended every year, preferably before the start of flu season. The Indian Medical Association (IMA) had said in 2015 that Influenza vaccines can prevent flu caused by human strains, which is "recommended for children above 6 months; Adults > 50 years of age; Patients with pulmonary, cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, neurologic, hematologic disorders and diabetes mellitus; pregnant females and Health care providers." "The inactivated vaccine can be given to the above groups. The Live attenuated influenza vaccine (intranasal spray) can be given only to persons aged 2-49 years (not to pregnant females)," the IMA added. NOTE: It's better to consult a doctor before getting an influenza vaccine. Speak with a healthcare provider first if you have specific allergies, comorbidities, a history of severe reactions, or an acute moderate-to-severe illness with a fever. When to take the vaccine? It takes about two weeks after vaccination for antibodies to develop and provide protection against influenza virus infection. In the meantime, you are still at risk of getting the flu. That's why it's better to get vaccinated early in the fall, before the flu season really gets underway. What if you are already sick with the H1N1 flu? If you have a fever, you should wait until it is gone before getting a flu shot, Max Healthcare stated. It explained that one can get a flu shot if they have a respiratory illness without a fever or another mild illness. According to the sources, the influenza strains currently circulating in the country are well matched with the vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere. AI Summary AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors Indian health authorities confirm no new H1N1 strain circulates despite rising cases in Delhi and India; current viruses match vaccine strains, surveillance continues, and medical consultation is advised for severe symptoms. Seasonal influenza, including H1N1, is generally self-limiting. Common symptoms include fever, cough, headache and body ache, with most patients recovering with adequate care and rest. However, young children, elderly people and those with underlying health conditions face a higher risk of complications. The Influenza A (H1N1) pdm09 viruses currently circulating in India belong to the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1) pdm09-like strain, the ICMR sources said. The viruses fall under clade 6B.1A.5a2a and subclade D.3.1.1 and have been circulating since 2025. People experiencing persistent, worsening or severe symptoms have been advised to consult a doctor promptly. Authorities are continuing to monitor the situation through regular surveillance and are taking necessary public health measures. Delhi has recorded more than 2,300 Influenza-A cases so far this year, including over 1,777 H1N1 cases as of Friday. The health department reported 114 H1N1 cases on Thursday alone. The Delhi government has issued a health advisory urging residents to maintain respiratory hygiene, avoid crowded places and seek medical attention when necessary. Also Read Delhi Sees Rise in H1N1 Cases: Symptoms, Spread, Treatment and Prevention Union Health Minister J P Nadda on Friday reviewed the H1N1 situation and preparedness across the country, with particular focus on Delhi. He called for continued vigilance, robust surveillance and proactive preparedness. Delhi Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh also attended the meeting. Nadda reviewed national surveillance and epidemiological trends, including influenza-like illness (ILI) and severe acute respiratory infection (SARI), along with testing, laboratory surveillance and the preparedness of healthcare facilities to manage seasonal influenza cases. He stressed the importance of closely monitoring influenza trends and ensuring the timely detection and management of any unusual increase or clustering of cases. The preparedness of healthcare facilities in Delhi was also assessed, including the availability of hospital beds, critical care facilities, oxygen-supported beds, ventilators, essential medicines, diagnostic services and other key supplies. Us Authors Submissions Style Guide Privacy Policy Terms and Conditions Cookie Policy Refund Policy Connect Subscribe Health ICMR says no new H1N1 strain as swine flu cases rise in India By News Desk Posted on 24 August 2026 Representative image: Influenza vaccine syringes, 16 October 2024. [Wikimedia Commons] Share Tweet Share Share Email Comments India is experiencing an increased number of H1N1 swine flu cases but the country is not facing the threat of a new strain of the virus, scientists from the Indian Council of Medical Research said. The currently available influenza vaccines also continue to be effective against circulating strains of the virus, The Hindu reported. Viruses such as the Influenza A (H1N1) pdm09 are in circulation in the country that are similar to the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1) pdm09-like strain, which has been prevalent in the country since 2025, ICMR reported. These viruses have also shown a strong match against vaccine strains that have been recommended for use in the northern hemisphere. “There is no need to panic,” officials with the ICMR have said. “Seasonal influenza, such as H1N1, is typically a mild condition that is self-limiting” ICMR officials said other common symptoms include cough, headache and body aches. Most people recover within a few days with proper care, adequate rest and treatment. This year, more than 1,777 cases have been observed in the country’s capital, Delhi alone and that is with the broader jump in influenza cases, information coming out of the Health Department indicates. Discover more City & Local Guides journalism Politics According to the ICMR, the elderly and young children with any particular health issue or an age that puts them in an at-risk group need more attention when it comes to complications associated with H1N1. “Anybody who has these particular conditions that do not seem to be improving or is going from bad to worse ought to consult a doctor.” The federal government is continuing its overall observation of influenza activity but remains focused on awareness over worry. Pradesh Teachers Delhi MLA Accident Navdeep Suri Nagpur Chlorine Leak Bengaluru logs 2,070 flu cases, 80% of 2025 tally already TNN / Aug 24, 2026, 12:11 IST Comments Share AA +Text Size Small Medium Large Bengaluru has experienced a significant increase in influenza cases this year, with over 2,000 confirmed, marking a higher figure than in previous years BENGALURU: Influenza cases in Bengaluru have already crossed the 2,000-mark this year, with 2,070 laboratory-confirmed cases recorded in the Greater Bengaluru area till August 22 — nearly 80% of the cases reported in the whole of 2025 and 74% higher than the corresponding annual figure for 2024.According to data released by the state health department on Monday, Greater Bengaluru recorded 2,070 influenza-positive cases till August 22, compared with 2,587 cases during all of 2025 and 1,189 in 2024. The figures indicate a substantial rise even before the current monsoon influenza season has run its course.Bengaluru Urban has also reported 1,011 cases so far this year, against 961 in 2025 and 991 in 2024. Bengaluru Rural and Bengaluru South have recorded 26 cases each till August 22.Across Karnataka, 4,212 laboratory-confirmed influenza cases have been reported in 2026 so far, compared with 4,583 cases in the whole of 2025 and 3,903 in 2024. The cases have been reported from 32 districts, according to surveillance data from the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP).The health department, however, said the current rise is part of the usual seasonal pattern and does not indicate an outbreak. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like Full Mouth Dental Implants Cost Without Insurance (Take A Look)FAQArena | Full Mouth Implants Learn More Undo Karnataka generally sees two seasonal peaks in influenza cases — between January and March and again between July and September.The department said surveillance of influenza-like illness (ILI) and severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) has been strengthened through designated sentinel sites, the ICMR-NCDC pan-respiratory virus surveillance network and Viral Research and Diagnostic Laboratories. It said laboratories have been equipped with adequate consumables for timely sample collection and testing.Following a review meeting chaired by Health Minister U T Khader with senior district health officials on Monday, health facilities have also been advised to maintain adequate stocks of essential supplies, including PPE, N95 masks and oseltamivir. Healthcare workers have been sensitised to the early recognition and management of ILI and SARI cases.Private hospitals and healthcare facilities have been asked to follow prescribed protocols for screening, testing and treatment of H1N1 cases and report cases through the IHIP platform.The department has advised people with symptoms to avoid crowded places, practise respiratory and hand hygiene, and avoid self-medication. It has also urged symptomatic people to seek medical care early, particularly to protect high-risk groups.Officials said the public need not panic, stressing that seasonal influenza can be prevented and managed with early detection, timely treatment and appropriate precautions.
